The first element is the name of the note g. The letter derives from Latin G, a modification of C, from Etruscan 𐌂 (c), from Ancient Greek Γ (G), from Phoenician 𐤂 (g).

Its musical sense is modelled on Italian chiave and French clef (“key; clef”).

27078.etyen:
Borrowed from Greenlandic inuit (“people”), the plural of inuk (“person”), from Proto-Inuit *inuɣ (“person”), from Proto-Eskimo *iŋuɣ (“human being”). In Norwegian, the borrowed plural form was reinterpreted as a singular count noun.
The Norwegian spelling with final -tt probably arose by analogy with -itt (“inhabitant- or member-forming suffix”), as in israelitt (“Israelite”), semitt (“Semite”) and arendalitt (“person from Arendal”).
Compare the parallel borrowings Norwegian Nynorsk inuitt, Danish inuit, Swedish inuit, German Inuit and English Inuit.

Borrowed from Romanian Jupiter (“Jupiter, Romanian seaside resort”), itself named after Jupiter (“Jupiter, the planet”).

It belongs to a deliberately astronomical series of neighbouring resort names which includes Neptun, Venus and Saturn, all named after planets; Romanian sources commonly refer to these resorts collectively as the “planets” of the coast.

1004998.etyen: Compound of gjæring (“fermentation”) + ambar (“wooden pail, wooden container”), with linking -s- (“interfix”), literally “fermentation ambar”.
